text: This lab is a worked written scenario — there's no ServiceNow instance to click through here. A team maintains the Equipment Checkout application, the same scoped application Course 6 introduced and this course's own capstone has been building toward. Their pipeline lives in GitHub Actions, connected to ServiceNow DevOps the way Lesson 18 described: every pull request triggers a build, then runs the application's ATF suite from Chapter 4, then deploys once the PR merges, reporting each stage back to ServiceNow. Two pull requests land in the same week. Walk through both.

The first PR fixes a cosmetic bug: a confusing field label on the checkout form, and a validation message that fired on the wrong condition for the equipment return date. The pipeline builds cleanly, the full ATF suite runs — including a new UI test added specifically for the corrected message — and every test passes. This change touches presentation and validation messaging only, nothing in approval routing or the data model. That combination, narrow functional scope plus direct, passing test coverage of exactly what changed, is what a pre-approved Standard Change template exists for. ServiceNow DevOps's automatic Change Request can legitimately move through that template: fast, low-friction, and still a real governed record.

The second PR touches something more consequential: the server-side logic deciding which manager has to approve a checkout request above a dollar threshold, after a reorganization left the old logic routing some high-value requests to a manager without authority over that equipment category. The pipeline builds cleanly, and the ATF suite, including the server-side tests covering approval logic, passes.

Passing tests here mean exactly one thing: the code does what the existing tests check for. They don't mean the new routing rule is correct for every real scenario the business cares about, and approval routing above a dollar threshold is exactly where a subtle mistake has real financial and audit consequences. This is a change with low technical-risk evidence but high business risk — and even with every test green, it belongs in front of the CAB, as a Normal Change, not fast-tracked through a Standard Change template just because the pipeline turned green.

Same application, same pipeline, same week, same ATF discipline — two different, correct outcomes. The deciding factor was never whether the pipeline succeeded. It was what the change actually touched, and whether the test coverage that passed was evidence about the part of the system that actually carries the business risk.

That closes this chapter's core tension between velocity and control. Next, Chapter 6 turns to deployment planning itself: planning a real deployment for a scoped application before it ever reaches production.
